\paragraph{Non-triviality of death dominance.}
Three qualitatively different interventions all fail to achieve deterministic-level safety (16.3\%). Brute-force retry provides no benefit (40.9\% $\approx$ baseline 42.9\%, Fisher exact $p > 0.6$). $10{\times}$ capability scaling moderately reduces death rate (${\sim}$51\% $\rightarrow$ ${\sim}$37\%, $\Delta \approx -14$~pp) but leaves a ${>}20$~pp gap to deterministic. Self-correction via Reflexion achieves comparable reduction on death-prone tasks (${\sim}$51\% $\rightarrow$ ${\sim}$35\%, $\Delta \approx -17$~pp) but cannot close the gap either. That scaling and Reflexion yield comparable reductions on the same task set (${\sim}$14~pp vs.\ ${\sim}$17~pp) through entirely different mechanisms, yet neither approaches deterministic-level safety, constitutes the strongest evidence that death dominance is a structural property of the environment rather than an agent-level deficiency. \texttt{find-non-living-thing} exhibits 0\% death across all conditions, confirming that death risk is task-specific.

Stronger backbones lower death rates but do not eliminate death dominance: Qwen2.5-72B reduces aggregate death from ${\sim}$51\% to ${\sim}$37\% ($-14$~pp), yet the gap to deterministic (16.3\%) remains ${>}20$~pp. The Llama pilot ($\delta = +34.3\%$) versus Qwen-7B ($\delta = +26.6\%$) is consistent in the capability-increase direction. Preliminary evidence (Qwen2.5-0.5B, $N{=}15$) suggests the relationship is non-monotonic: very weak models exhibit low death rates from inability to reach dangerous states. We predict that in any environment where one modality triggers irreversible catastrophic failures with severe penalties, death avoidance will dominate routing signal; self-correction mechanisms can selectively reduce death-driven signal but cannot eliminate structural death dominance.

\section{Introduction}

Large language models deployed as interactive agents must repeatedly decide \emph{how} to compute: reason internally, or delegate to an external tool.
A Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct agent navigating ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022}, a text-based science simulation with 30 task types, faces this choice at every step. Tracking temperature thresholds, container states, and multi-step procedures via internal reasoning is error-prone: the model may hallucinate that water has boiled when the stove was never activated, or that an object has been moved when the action was invalid. Deterministic external computation (environment simulators, code interpreters) eliminates such hallucinations via exact state transitions. The practical question for agent design is therefore: \emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus reasoning internally?}

Existing routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision.
Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} teaches models to insert API calls when doing so reduces perplexity; ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} selects among heterogeneous modules (search, code, vision) per subtask.
More recent adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \cite{mtrouter-2026}.
The shared assumption is that routing signal stems from diverse sources (accuracy, latency, capability matching) and that a learned router can exploit this signal to improve over any fixed strategy.
But this assumption has never been systematically verified: \emph{what actually drives the value of routing decisions in interactive environments?}
If routing value traces to a single failure mode, practitioners can replace complex learned routers with simpler safety-aware policies at lower computational cost and deployment risk.

We propose a \emph{formal diagnostic framework} for answering this question. \section{Introduction}

Large language models deployed as interactive agents must repeatedly decide \emph{how} to compute: reason internally, or delegate to an external tool.
A Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct agent navigating ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022}, a text-based science simulation with 30 task types, faces this choice at every step. Tracking temperature thresholds, container states, and multi-step procedures via internal reasoning is error-prone: the model may hallucinate that water has boiled when the stove was never activated, or that an object has been moved when the action was invalid. Deterministic external computation (environment simulators, code interpreters) eliminates such hallucinations via exact state transitions. The practical question for agent design is therefore: \emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus reasoning internally?}

Existing routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision.
Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} teaches models to insert API calls when doing so reduces perplexity; ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} selects among heterogeneous modules (search, code, vision) per subtask.
More recent adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \cite{mtrouter-2026}.
The shared assumption is that routing signal stems from diverse sources (accuracy, latency, capability matching) and that a learned router can exploit this signal to improve over any fixed strategy.
But this assumption has never been systematically verified: \emph{what actually drives the value of routing decisions in interactive environments?}
If routing value traces to a single failure mode, practitioners can replace complex learned routers with simpler safety-aware policies at lower computational cost and deployment risk.

We propose a \emph{formal diagnostic framework} for answering this question. The framework comprises (i)~episode-level counterfactual labeling under pure strategies (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:labeling}), and (ii)~the Death Avoidance Factor (DAF), a penalty-dependent metric that decomposes the routing score gap into death-avoidance and non-death components (\S\ref{sec:daf}). Applied to ScienceWorld, \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry} (75 of 95), a penalty-independent finding that holds regardless of how death is penalized. Under ScienceWorld's specific penalty structure ($P{=}100$), the penalty-weighted DAF reaches $90.4\%$ (95\% CI: $[81.6\%, 98.8\%]$), consistent with the predicted value from observed $\delta{=}0.265$ and $P{=}100$.
The internal strategy's hallucination-induced failures trigger catastrophic agent death (a $-100$ penalty), while the deterministic strategy survives the same episodes.
Once death episodes are removed, the performance gap collapses to $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$. A per-task consistency check ($r = 0.97$) confirms that the near-perfect correlation is a mathematical consequence of death dominance when $P$ is constant (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}).

This framework addresses a methodological gap.
The standard approach to generating routing labels, per-step oracle comparison, degenerates under sparse rewards.
In ScienceWorld, non-zero reward arrives only at episode termination; 97.4\% of steps (across 11 prescreened task types) produce identical scores regardless of modality, so no step-level signal exists (\S\ref{sec:collection}).
Keyword-based heuristics also fail structurally, as ScienceWorld actions lack science-specific terminology (\S\ref{sec:baselines}).
Our counterfactual approach runs complete episodes under pure-internal (ReAct \cite{react-2023}) and pure-deterministic strategies, then compares episode outcomes to generate routing labels (\S\ref{sec:collection}). The framework is applicable to any environment with controllable modality comparison and binary catastrophic outcomes, requiring only paired episode outcomes under two modalities.

Two cross-context checks probe the specificity of this finding.
First, a MATH Level~4--5 evaluation ($N{=}795$ problems, code interpreter as deterministic modality) confirms no routing signal without catastrophic failure: internal reasoning and code interpretation achieve near-identical accuracy ($73.5\%$ vs.\ $73.0\%$, $p = 0.81$).
Second, a preliminary cross-model pilot with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (7 task types, $N{=}70$) shows direction-consistent death patterns, with a larger death-rate differential ($+34.3\%$ vs.\ $+26.6\%$ for Qwen; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model}).
Agent improvement baselines confirm that death dominance is structural: retry does not reduce death rate, $10{\times}$ model scaling (72B) moderately reduces it but leaves an ${\sim}$18~pp gap to deterministic, and Reflexion~\citep{reflexion-2023} only partially reduces it (\S\ref{sec:agent-improvement}).
An exploratory router (Qwen3 LoRA, 0.6B--4B) yields flat step-level balanced accuracy ($56$--$59\%$); at episode level, only 4B exceeds the always-deterministic baseline (\S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{A formal episode-level counterfactual framework (Algorithm~\ref{alg:labeling}) with dual penalty-independent and penalty-dependent metrics} for decomposing routing signal into death-avoidance and non-death components. The framework applies to any environment with controllable modality comparison and binary catastrophic outcomes (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:daf}).

    \item \textbf{Empirical application to ScienceWorld} revealing that 78.9\% of non-tie routing labels are driven by death asymmetry (penalty-independent), with DAF $= 90.4\%$ at $P{=}100$ (penalty-dependent). Agent improvement baselines (retry, $10{\times}$ scaling, Reflexion) confirm this is structural: none approach deterministic-level safety. Router training yields flat step-level accuracy across scales ($56$--$59\%$); death dominance renders always-deterministic near-optimal (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}--\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

\end{enumerate}
